entries.meaning: The rate at which something speeds up. ---
examples: This little car has surprising acceleration.
Acceleration is measured in meters per second squared.
The graph shows the acceleration over the first ten seconds.

entries.meaning: The act or state of moving. ---
examples: Newton's laws describe the motion of objects.
The camera captures the motion of the bird's wings.
The bus was already in motion when he jumped off.

entries.meaning: The force a moving object has because of its mass and its speed. ---
examples: A truck has far more momentum than a bicycle.
The sled lost momentum on the flat ground.
In a collision, the total momentum stays the same.

entries.meaning: The force that slows down two surfaces rubbing against each other. ---
examples: Friction between the tires and the road slows the car.
Oil reduces the friction inside the engine.
Without friction, you couldn't walk across the floor.

entries.meaning: The tendency of an object to keep doing whatever it is already doing. ---
examples: Inertia is why you lurch forward when the bus stops.
A heavy flywheel has a lot of inertia.
The seatbelt works against your body's inertia.

entries.meaning: Tension has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The cable snapped under the tension.
Adjust the tension on the belt before you start the motor.
Tension in the string keeps the weight from falling.
You could feel the tension in the room.
There has been tension between the two departments for years.
A walk usually gets rid of the tension in my shoulders.

senses.head: The pulling force in a stretched rope, wire, or spring
examples: The cable snapped under the tension.
Adjust the tension on the belt before you start the motor.
Tension in the string keeps the weight from falling.

senses.head: Strain in a person or between people
examples: You could feel the tension in the room.
There has been tension between the two departments for years.
A walk usually gets rid of the tension in my shoulders.

entries.meaning: The forward force produced by an engine or a rocket. ---
examples: The engines produce enough thrust to lift the rocket.
The pilot cut the thrust just before landing.
Each booster adds thrust at liftoff.

entries.meaning: The pressing of something into a smaller space. ---
examples: The compression of the gas raised its temperature.
Concrete is very strong under compression.
Low compression in one cylinder explains the misfire.

entries.meaning: The process of burning fuel together with oxygen. ---
examples: Combustion releases heat and carbon dioxide.
The engine runs on internal combustion.
Without oxygen, combustion stops immediately.

entries.meaning: The hot glowing gas you see when something burns. ---
examples: Hold the wire in the flame until it glows.
The flames spread to the next room.
A blue flame means the gas is burning cleanly.

entries.meaning: A tiny piece of burning material or a small flash of electricity. ---
examples: A single spark set off the whole fire.
Sparks flew when the metal hit the grinder.
The plug fires a spark on every cycle.

entries.meaning: The change of a liquid into a gas. ---
examples: Evaporation cools your skin when you sweat.
The puddle disappeared through evaporation.
Cover the dish to prevent evaporation.

entries.meaning: The change of a gas into a liquid, or the drops this leaves behind. ---
examples: Condensation formed on the cold glass.
Wipe the condensation off the window.
Clouds form by the condensation of water vapor.

entries.meaning: The process of getting larger in size. ---
examples: Heat causes the expansion of most metals.
The bridge has gaps to allow for expansion.
The expansion of the gas pushed the piston out.

entries.meaning: The process of getting smaller in size. ---
examples: Cooling leads to the contraction of the metal.
The rails leave room for contraction in winter.
Contraction pulled the seams apart.

entries.meaning: The movement of heat through a liquid or gas as it circulates. ---
examples: This oven heats food by convection.
Warm air rises by convection.
Convection currents keep the water mixing.

entries.meaning: Energy that travels out from a source as waves or particles. ---
examples: The lab shields its workers from radiation.
Radiation from the sun warms the earth.
They measured the radiation around the reactor.

entries.meaning: A complete path that electricity can flow around. ---
examples: The circuit is broken somewhere near the switch.
Never work on a live circuit.
Both circuits are protected by fuses.

entries.meaning: A piece of metal that attracts iron and steel. ---
examples: Hold the magnet near the paper clips.
We stuck the drawing to the fridge with a magnet.
Two magnets will push apart if you flip one around.

entries.meaning: The force by which magnets attract or push away other objects. ---
examples: Magnetism and electricity are closely related.
Heating the metal destroyed its magnetism.
The class covered magnetism last week.

entries.meaning: A material that does not let electricity or heat pass through. ---
examples: Rubber is a good insulator.
The handle is wrapped in an insulator.
Ceramic insulators hold the power lines away from the pole.

entries.meaning: The thin wire inside a light bulb that glows when it heats up. ---
examples: The filament burned out after a year.
You can see the filament through the clear glass.
Old bulbs used tungsten filaments.

entries.meaning: A device that raises or lowers the voltage of an electric supply. ---
examples: The transformer on the pole blew during the storm.
A small transformer steps the voltage down to twelve volts.
Both transformers were replaced last year.

entries.meaning: A fast shaking movement back and forth. ---
examples: You can feel the vibration through the floor.
Vibrations from the engine loosened the bolt.
Rubber pads absorb most of the vibration.

entries.meaning: Reflection has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She saw her reflection in the store window.
The reflection off the water was blinding.
We measured the reflections of sound in the empty hall.
On reflection, I think we should wait.
The essay collects her reflections on twenty years of teaching.
He caught his reflection in the shop window.

senses.head: Light or sound bouncing back from a surface, or the image this makes
examples: She saw her reflection in the store window.
The reflection off the water was blinding.
We measured the reflections of sound in the empty hall.

senses.head: Serious thought about something, or an image thrown back by a mirror or water
examples: On reflection, I think we should wait.
The essay collects her reflections on twenty years of teaching.
He caught his reflection in the shop window.

entries.meaning: The bending of light as it passes from one material into another. ---
examples: Refraction makes the straw look broken in the glass.
A lens works by refraction.
Refraction in the atmosphere shifts the star's position slightly.

entries.meaning: A clear block of glass that splits light into colors. ---
examples: Hold the prism up in the sunlight.
The prism spread the beam into a rainbow.
Two glass prisms sat on the lab bench.

entries.meaning: A device that produces a narrow, very bright beam of light. ---
examples: The laser cuts right through sheet metal.
Don't point the laser at anyone's eyes.
Surgeons use lasers for some eye operations.

entries.meaning: Anything that has mass and takes up space. ---
examples: Solids, liquids, and gases are all forms of matter.
Matter cannot be created or destroyed.
The telescope detects matter falling into the black hole.

entries.meaning: A substance that keeps its own shape, such as ice or wood. ---
examples: Ice is water in the form of a solid.
Solids usually expand a little when they are heated.
The mixture separates into a solid and a liquid.

entries.meaning: A very hot gas whose particles carry an electric charge. ---
examples: Stars are made of plasma.
The lamp glows because the gas turns into plasma.
Plasma is often called the fourth state of matter.

entries.meaning: A liquid or gas that flows and takes the shape of its container. ---
examples: Brake fluid should be changed every few years.
Both gases and liquids are fluids.
The pump moves fluid through the pipes.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: The smallest unit of a chemical element. ---
examples: A water molecule contains three atoms.
Every atom has a nucleus at its center.
The scientists managed to split the atom.

entries.meaning: A group of atoms joined together, the smallest piece of a compound. ---
examples: A water molecule is two hydrogens and one oxygen.
Molecules move faster when you heat them.
The drug attaches to one molecule at a time.

entries.meaning: A tiny particle with a negative charge that moves around an atom. ---
examples: Electric current is a flow of electrons.
An electron is far lighter than a proton.
This metal gives up one electron easily.

entries.meaning: A particle with a positive charge found in the center of an atom. ---
examples: Each proton carries a positive charge.
Carbon has six protons.
The number of protons decides which element it is.

entries.meaning: A particle with no electric charge found in the center of an atom. ---
examples: A neutron weighs about the same as a proton.
The nucleus holds both protons and neutrons.
Free neutrons keep the reaction going.

entries.meaning: An extremely small piece of matter. ---
examples: Dust particles floated in the sunlight.
The filter traps any particle larger than a micron.
Physicists study how one particle hits another.

entries.meaning: An atom that carries an electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons. ---
examples: Salt splits into two ions when it dissolves.
A sodium ion has a positive charge.
The ions carry the current through the liquid.
entries.contrast: Not the same word as iron, which is EYE-urn.

entries.meaning: A form of an element that has a different number of neutrons. ---
examples: Carbon has several isotopes.
One isotope of hydrogen is used in reactors.
Doctors use a radioactive isotope to trace blood flow.

entries.meaning: A metal made by mixing two or more metals together. ---
examples: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
The frame is made from a light aluminum alloy.
Different alloys melt at different temperatures.
entries.contrast: The noun is AL-oy; the rare verb is uh-LOY.

entries.meaning: A liquid with something dissolved in it. ---
examples: Pour the salt solution into the beaker.
Prepare two solutions of different strength.
The solution turned blue when we added the powder.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A liquid that can dissolve other substances. ---
examples: Water is the most common solvent of all.
Use a solvent to get the paint off.
Some solvents give off dangerous fumes.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A compound formed when a substance combines with oxygen. ---
examples: Rust is an oxide of iron.
The white powder is zinc oxide.
Several oxides formed on the surface.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A compound of chlorine with another element, such as table salt. ---
examples: Table salt is sodium chloride.
The well water contains too much chloride.
Chloride levels in the sample were high.

entries.meaning: A material made of very long chains of repeating molecules. ---
examples: Most plastics are polymers.
The coating is a flexible polymer.
New polymers are replacing metal parts.

entries.meaning: A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. ---
examples: The reaction needs a catalyst to go quickly.
Platinum acts as a catalyst in the exhaust system.
Enzymes are biological catalysts.

entries.meaning: A substance made by living cells that speeds up a chemical reaction. ---
examples: This enzyme breaks down starch.
Digestive enzymes work best at body temperature.
Heat destroys the enzyme.

entries.meaning: Concentration has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Increase the concentration of the acid slightly.
High concentrations of salt kill the plants.
The concentration dropped as we added water.
The noise from the street broke my concentration.
Chess takes hours of concentration.
His concentration slipped in the last mile.

senses.head: How much of a substance is present in a mixture
examples: Increase the concentration of the acid slightly.
High concentrations of salt kill the plants.
The concentration dropped as we added water.

senses.head: The act of giving all your attention to one thing
examples: The noise from the street broke my concentration.
Chess takes hours of concentration.
His concentration slipped in the last mile.

entries.meaning: How acid something is. ---
examples: Test the acidity of the soil before planting.
Lemon juice adds acidity to the sauce.
The acidity of the rain has damaged the stone.

entries.meaning: How thick a liquid is and how slowly it flows. ---
examples: Honey has a very high viscosity.
Cold weather increases the oil's viscosity.
We measured the viscosity at three temperatures.

entries.meaning: How free a substance is from other materials mixed into it. ---
examples: The lab checks the purity of every batch.
Gold is sold by weight and purity.
A purity above ninety-nine percent is required.

entries.meaning: How well a material carries electricity or heat. ---
examples: Silver has the highest electrical conductivity of any metal.
Salt raises the water's conductivity.
We measured the conductivity of each sample.

entries.meaning: A process in which substances change into different substances. ---
examples: The reaction gives off a lot of heat.
Some reactions will not start without a catalyst.
Mixing the two powders starts the reaction.

entries.meaning: A reaction in which a substance combines with oxygen. ---
examples: Rust is caused by oxidation.
The coating slows the oxidation of the metal.
Oxidation is what turns a cut apple brown.

entries.meaning: The slow damage caused when a metal reacts with air or water. ---
examples: Salt on the roads speeds up corrosion.
There was heavy corrosion around the battery terminals.
Paint protects the steel from corrosion.

entries.meaning: The gradual breaking down of a substance or of a radioactive material. ---
examples: Radioactive decay releases energy over time.
The rate of decay is measured in half-lives.
Bacteria cause decay in dead plants.

entries.meaning: The splitting of an atom's nucleus, which releases energy. ---
examples: Nuclear fission powers the plant.
The fission of uranium releases enormous energy.
The reactor controls the rate of fission.

entries.meaning: The joining of two atomic nuclei, which releases a huge amount of energy. ---
examples: The sun is powered by fusion.
Fusion would give us almost limitless energy.
Scientists have struggled for decades to control fusion.

entries.meaning: A large machine in which nuclear reactions are controlled to make energy. ---
examples: The reactor was shut down for maintenance.
Two reactors supply the whole city.
Water cools the core of the reactor.

entries.meaning: A very light gas that is used to fill balloons. ---
examples: The balloons are filled with helium.
Helium makes your voice sound funny.
There is a worldwide shortage of helium.

entries.meaning: A greenish gas used to kill germs in water. ---
examples: The pool smells strongly of chlorine.
Chlorine is added to drinking water.
Too much chlorine irritates your eyes.

entries.meaning: A soft silver-white metal that is one half of ordinary salt. ---
examples: The label lists the amount of sodium per serving.
Sodium reacts violently with water.
Cut back on sodium if your blood pressure is high.

entries.meaning: A silver-white metal found in bones, teeth, and milk. ---
examples: Milk is a good source of calcium.
Her doctor told her to take more calcium.
Calcium builds up inside the pipes.

entries.meaning: A soft silver-white metal that the body needs in small amounts. ---
examples: Bananas contain a lot of potassium.
Low potassium can cause muscle cramps.
The fertilizer supplies nitrogen and potassium.

entries.meaning: A light silver-white metal that burns with a bright white flame. ---
examples: Magnesium burns with a blinding white light.
The frame is made of a magnesium alloy.
She takes magnesium for her leg cramps.

entries.meaning: A heavy radioactive metal used as nuclear fuel. ---
examples: The plant runs on enriched uranium.
Uranium is mined in several western states.
They found traces of uranium in the soil.

entries.meaning: A soft black form of carbon used in pencils. ---
examples: Pencil leads are made of graphite and clay.
Graphite conducts electricity.
The rods are coated with graphite.

entries.meaning: Petroleum has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Gasoline is made from petroleum.
Petroleum prices rose again this month.
Most plastics are a petroleum product.
Plastic is made from petroleum.
The company has been drilling for petroleum since the 1920s.
Almost every part of that engine runs on petroleum products.

senses.head: The thick oil taken from underground and refined into fuel
examples: Gasoline is made from petroleum.
Petroleum prices rose again this month.
Most plastics are a petroleum product.

senses.head: The thick dark oil pumped from underground that fuels and plastics are made from
examples: Plastic is made from petroleum.
The company has been drilling for petroleum since the 1920s.
Almost every part of that engine runs on petroleum products.

entries.meaning: The gray powder that is left after something has burned. ---
examples: There was ash all over the grill.
Volcanic ash closed the airport for two days.
Sweep the ash out of the fireplace.
entries.contrast: Ashes is a separate word, used for the remains of a fire or a body.

entries.meaning: The fine black powder left behind by smoke. ---
examples: The chimney was black with soot.
Soot had settled on every surface in the room.
He wiped the soot off the glass.
entries.contrast: Rhymes with foot, not with suit.

entries.meaning: A small amount of something left behind after a process. ---
examples: A sticky residue stayed on the glass.
Wash off any residue before you weigh it.
Pesticide residues were found on the fruit.

entries.meaning: Solid material that settles at the bottom of a liquid. ---
examples: Sediment collected at the bottom of the tube.
The river carries sediment downstream.
Pour it off slowly and leave the sediment behind.

entries.meaning: An informal word for a laboratory. ---
examples: We ran the test in the lab.
Her lab is on the third floor.
Most of the labs close at six.

entries.meaning: A thin tube used to move an exact amount of liquid. ---
examples: Use a pipette to add exactly five milliliters.
Rinse the pipette between samples.
The pipettes are in the top drawer.

entries.meaning: A cone-shaped tube used for pouring liquid into a narrow opening. ---
examples: Use a funnel so you don't spill it.
The funnel was lined with filter paper.
Two plastic funnels hung by the sink.

entries.meaning: A small tube with a rubber bulb for releasing liquid one drop at a time. ---
examples: Add the dye with a dropper.
The dropper holds about a milliliter.
Both droppers were labeled with tape.

entries.meaning: A plug of rubber, glass, or cork that closes a bottle or a tube. ---
examples: Push the stopper firmly into the flask.
The stopper popped out from the pressure.
Rubber stoppers come in several sizes.

entries.meaning: A device that removes solid pieces or unwanted material from a liquid or gas. ---
examples: Pour the mixture through a paper filter.
Change the air filter once a year.
The filters clogged after an hour.

entries.meaning: A very thin layer that lets some substances pass through it. ---
examples: Water passes through the membrane but salt does not.
The membrane tore under the pressure.
Cell membranes control what goes in and out.

entries.meaning: A thin instrument used to measure or examine something. ---
examples: Insert the temperature probe into the sample.
The probe sends data back every second.
Two probes recorded the voltage.

entries.meaning: A device that finds the presence of something such as smoke or radiation. ---
examples: The smoke detector went off at midnight.
The metal detector beeped at his belt buckle.
Radiation detectors line the corridor.

entries.meaning: A machine that turns fuel or electricity into movement. ---
examples: The engine burns a mixture of fuel and air.
Both engines shut down at the same moment.
A diesel engine is more efficient than a gasoline one.

entries.meaning: A machine with blades that spin to produce power. ---
examples: Steam drives the turbine.
Wind turbines line the whole ridge.
The turbine generates enough power for a small town.

entries.meaning: A part that slides up and down inside a cylinder to create movement. ---
examples: The piston moves down as the gas expands.
One piston was badly scratched.
This engine has six pistons.

entries.meaning: Something you notice and write down while watching carefully. ---
examples: Write your observations in the notebook.
One observation did not fit the pattern.
The theory rests on years of careful observations.

entries.meaning: What you find out at the end of an experiment or test. ---
examples: The results surprised everyone in the lab.
We got the same result three times in a row.
Her results were published last spring.

entries.meaning: Data has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The data shows a clear trend.
We collected data for six months.
All of the data is stored on the server.
We lost three days of data.
The data shows a clear pattern.
They sell your data to advertisers.
I used up all my data watching videos.
The data shows a clear drop after March.
They collect data on everything you click.

senses.head: Facts and numbers collected for study
examples: The data shows a clear trend.
We collected data for six months.
All of the data is stored on the server.

senses.head: Facts and figures stored or processed by a computer
examples: We lost three days of data.
The data shows a clear pattern.
They sell your data to advertisers.

senses.head: Information stored or sent by a computer or phone
examples: I used up all my data watching videos.
The data shows a clear drop after March.
They collect data on everything you click.

entries.contrast: In American English data normally takes a singular verb: the data is.

entries.meaning: Principle has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The pump works on a very simple principle.
He explained the principle behind the experiment.
The same principles apply to gases and liquids.
She quit on principle rather than sign it.
He's a man of strong principles.
The principle is simple: never charge more than it costs.

senses.head: A basic scientific rule that explains how something works
examples: The pump works on a very simple principle.
He explained the principle behind the experiment.
The same principles apply to gases and liquids.

senses.head: A basic rule or belief that guides how a person behaves
examples: She quit on principle rather than sign it.
He's a man of strong principles.
The principle is simple: never charge more than it costs.

entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like principal, the head of a school.

entries.meaning: A mathematical statement that two amounts are equal. ---
examples: Solve the equation for the unknown value.
The equation balances on both sides.
These equations describe how the wave moves.

entries.meaning: A planned way of doing something. ---
examples: The scientific method starts with a question.
We tried a different method the second time.
Both methods gave the same answer.

entries.meaning: The set of steps you follow to do something correctly. ---
examples: Follow the safety procedure exactly.
The whole procedure takes about twenty minutes.
Lab procedures are posted on the wall.

entries.meaning: A particular skilled way of doing something. ---
examples: The new technique saves hours of work.
She developed a technique for growing the crystals.
Both techniques have their drawbacks.
entries.contrast: The -que ending is just a k sound: tek-NEEK.

entries.meaning: Variable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Change only one variable at a time.
Temperature was the one variable we controlled.
Too many variables make the results hard to read.
Give the variable a name that means something.
All these variables are global, which is asking for trouble.
The variable was never initialized.

senses.head: Something in an experiment that can change
examples: Change only one variable at a time.
Temperature was the one variable we controlled.
Too many variables make the results hard to read.

senses.head: A named place in a program where a value is stored
examples: Give the variable a name that means something.
All these variables are global, which is asking for trouble.
The variable was never initialized.

entries.meaning: A drawing that shows how two sets of numbers are related. ---
examples: Plot your results on a graph.
The graph shows a steady rise.
Both graphs use the same scale.
entries.contrast: The ph is pronounced like f.

entries.meaning: A scientist who studies chemical substances and reactions. ---
examples: A chemist analyzed the sample for us.
Chemists developed the new coating.
He worked as a chemist for a paint company.
entries.contrast: In America a chemist is a scientist; in Britain the word can also mean a pharmacist.

entries.meaning: A scientist who studies matter, energy, and forces.
examples: The physicist explained the results to the reporters.
Several physicists worked on the design.
She trained as a physicist before switching to medicine.
